Kubernetes API server overload: The API: Start with `apiserver_request_duration_seconds` and `apiserver_current_inflight_requests` metrics broken down by verb/resource to see which request type is dominating, and check API Priority and Fairness (APF) queue metrics (`apiserver_flowcontrol_*`) to see which FlowSchema/PriorityLevel is saturated - APF by default isolates well-behaved traffic from a noisy client, so a misbehaving controller usually shows up as one priority level being exhausted while others are fine. Cross-reference with audit logs filtered by user/service account to identify the specific client hammering the API (a controller stuck in a retry loop, a misconfigured watch without proper backoff), then contain it by adjusting its FlowSchema to a lower priority level or fixing/restarting the offending client - client-side throttling (adjusting QPS/burst settings on that client's kubeconfig) is the longer-term prevention.
Kubernetes etcd performance: A self-mana: Check `etcd_disk_wal_fsync_duration_seconds` and `etcd_disk_backend_commit_duration_seconds` first - etcd is extremely disk-latency sensitive, and slow fsync times (often from non-SSD storage or noisy-neighbor disk contention) are the most common root cause of both slow writes and spurious leader elections (a lagging follower missing heartbeats triggers unnecessary elections). Check database size against the configured quota (`etcd_mvcc_db_total_size_in_bytes`) and run `defrag` if fragmentation is high (large gap between logical size and allocated size) - during business hours defrag on the leader last, one member at a time, to avoid quorum loss. For recovery, always take a `etcdctl snapshot save` before any risky operation, and never restore from snapshot without confirming the target cluster's member IDs/URLs match, since a mismatched restore can silently create a split-brain cluster.
Kubernetes scheduler internals: Walk thr: The scheduler runs two phases per Pod: filtering (Predicates) eliminates nodes that can't run the Pod at all (insufficient resources, unsatisfied node affinity/taints, port conflicts), then scoring (Priorities) ranks the remaining feasible nodes (spreading for topology constraints, resource balance, image locality) and picks the highest-scoring one. If no node passes filtering, preemption kicks in - the scheduler looks for lower-PriorityClass Pods it could evict to make room, simulating whether evicting them would let the pending Pod fit, and only preempts if it actually resolves the scheduling failure. Topology spread constraints influence the scoring phase specifically, penalizing nodes that would create imbalance across the specified topology key (zone, hostname); scheduler profiles let you run multiple named scheduling configurations (different plugin sets/weights) for different workload classes within the same cluster.
Kubernetes scheduling deadlock: Several: This is almost always a fragmentation problem, not a true capacity shortage - aggregate free CPU/memory can be sufficient while no single node has enough contiguous capacity, or the free capacity is on nodes that fail the Pod's specific constraints. Check `kubectl describe pod` for the exact FailedScheduling reason per node (it lists why each node was rejected), common culprits being an unsatisfiable topology spread constraint combined with too few zones/nodes, a PVC that can only bind in a specific zone (topology-aware volume provisioning) where no schedulable node exists, or a taint with no matching toleration on otherwise-free nodes. If preemption should apply but isn't triggering, check whether the pending Pod's PriorityClass is actually higher than candidates, since preemption never evicts equal-or-higher priority Pods.
Kubernetes graceful termination: A servi: The classic race is that Kubernetes marks the Pod Terminating and sends SIGTERM to the container at the same moment it starts removing the Pod from Service endpoints - but endpoint removal propagation (to kube-proxy, and further to any external load balancer) is not instantaneous, so requests can still arrive briefly after the container has started shutting down. Fix with a `preStop` hook that sleeps for a few seconds before the container actually begins shutdown, giving endpoint removal time to propagate everywhere first, combined with the application handling SIGTERM by stopping *new* request acceptance immediately while finishing in-flight requests, and a `terminationGracePeriodSeconds` generous enough to cover both the preStop sleep and the longest reasonable in-flight request duration.
Kubernetes PDB failure scenario: A node: Check `kubectl get pdb` for `ALLOWED DISRUPTIONS` per PDB to see exactly which one is at zero, and cross-reference against actual replica health (a PDB blocking eviction because replicas are already degraded, e.g. one replica already down for an unrelated reason, is telling you correctly that evicting another would breach real availability, not being falsely conservative). If the PDB is correctly protecting real availability, the safe path is to first restore full replica health (fix whatever's actually degraded) rather than relaxing the PDB, or to temporarily scale up extra replicas beyond the normal count specifically to absorb the disruption headroom needed for the upgrade, then scale back down afterward - relaxing the PDB's `minAvailable` threshold itself should be a last resort reserved for cases where the PDB was simply set stricter than actually required.
Kubernetes HPA instability: An HPA rapid: First confirm every Pod backing the HPA has resource requests set correctly (HPA math divides usage by requests - missing or wildly inconsistent requests across replicas produces a noisy, unstable utilization signal even under genuinely steady load). Check metric freshness/staleness (metrics-server or the custom metrics pipeline lagging behind real load causes the HPA to react to outdated data, overshooting in both directions), and check whether the HPA's stabilization window is too short for the workload's natural traffic variance (a short window reacts to noise; widening it, or tuning scaling policies' max step size per period, dampens flapping). If latency stays unstable even once replica count stabilizes, the actual bottleneck may be downstream (a database or shared dependency that doesn't scale with the API tier), which HPA on the API tier alone can never fix.
Kubernetes KEDA event scaling: How would: Design consumers to be idempotent regardless of KEDA's scaling behavior (a message can always be redelivered/processed more than once in any queue-based system, scale-to-zero or not), since KEDA scaling replicas up and down doesn't itself guarantee exactly-once processing. Tune the KEDA ScaledObject's polling interval and cooldown period to avoid scale-to-zero introducing unacceptable cold-start latency for latency-sensitive queues (keep a minReplicaCount of 1 for those), and cap `maxReplicaCount` and consumer concurrency so a sudden queue depth spike can't scale consumers faster than the downstream system (a database, an external API) they call can actually absorb - pair this with backoff/circuit-breaking in the consumer itself so a downstream outage doesn't turn into a retry storm amplified by dozens of newly-scaled-up consumers all retrying simultaneously.
Kubernetes CNI debugging: Pod-to-pod tra: Same-node Pod traffic working while cross-node fails points strongly at the overlay/routing layer rather than the CNI's basic Pod networking setup - check whether the CNI uses encapsulation (VXLAN/IPIP) and whether an MTU mismatch is causing large packets to silently drop (a very common cause: the overlay adds encapsulation overhead, and if the Pod's effective MTU isn't reduced to account for it, larger packets fail while small ping packets succeed, creating a confusing partial-failure signature). Check node-to-node routing/firewall rules at the cloud level (a security group/firewall rule allowing traffic within a node but not between nodes' Pod CIDR ranges), NetworkPolicy scope (confirm it's not inadvertently restricting cross-node traffic specifically), and conntrack table health on nodes carrying heavy cross-node traffic - `tcpdump` on both the source and destination node's interfaces is the definitive way to see exactly where in the path the packet is being dropped.
Kubernetes DNS at scale: CoreDNS latency: Check the default `ndots:5` search-domain behavior first - many applications' DNS libraries generate multiple sequential lookups per actual query (trying each search domain suffix in turn before the final absolute lookup succeeds), amplifying real query volume several-fold, which becomes a serious problem at scale. Check CoreDNS's own resource limits/replica count (is it CPU-throttled or under-provisioned for the query volume) and whether its cache TTLs are tuned appropriately, check whether upstream resolver latency (for external domain lookups) is the actual bottleneck rather than CoreDNS itself, and deploy NodeLocal DNSCache (a per-node caching agent) to absorb the bulk of repeat queries locally without a network hop to CoreDNS at all - this is the standard fix once CoreDNS itself becomes a scaling bottleneck at high Pod density.
Kubernetes conntrack exhaustion: Service: Confirm via `conntrack -S` (or the node's `nf_conntrack_count` vs `nf_conntrack_max`) showing the table near its limit, alongside kernel logs showing 'nf_conntrack: table full, dropping packet' - this is invisible to typical Pod/node health checks since both the Pod and node process are fine, only new connection tracking is failing. Identify the traffic pattern causing it (very high connection churn - short-lived connections opened and closed rapidly, common with certain connection-pooling misconfigurations or a DDoS-like retry storm) via per-Pod/per-node connection counts. Mitigate immediately by raising `nf_conntrack_max` (a sysctl, doable via a DaemonSet with privileged access to tune node kernel parameters) and prevent recurrence by fixing the root cause of excessive connection churn (proper connection pooling/keep-alive in the client) rather than just continuing to raise the ceiling indefinitely.
Kubernetes Gateway API migration: How wo: Run both in parallel during migration rather than a hard cutover: deploy Gateway API resources (Gateway + HTTPRoute) alongside existing Ingress resources, initially pointing at the same backend Services, and validate routing/TLS behavior matches exactly using a small percentage of shadow or canary traffic before shifting real users. Migrate one route/host at a time (not all at once) so a problem is isolated and easily rolled back (revert to the Ingress-based path for just that host), keep the same observability/dashboards mapped to both paths during the transition so you can directly compare behavior, and only decommission the old Ingress resources once every route has been validated on Gateway API for a reasonable soak period.
Kubernetes zero-trust networking: Design: Start with a default-deny NetworkPolicy per namespace (deny all ingress and egress), then explicitly allow only what's needed: DNS (egress to kube-dns/CoreDNS on port 53, almost always the first thing forgotten and the most common cause of everything breaking after enabling default-deny), specific external API egress allow-listed by destination, and intra-namespace/cross-namespace traffic explicitly permitted only where a real dependency exists. Layer a service mesh (Istio/Linkerd) for mTLS and finer-grained L7 authorization on top of NetworkPolicy's L3/L4 controls. Test policies in a non-production namespace first with the same topology, and maintain a documented, audited break-glass process (a separate, tightly-controlled policy or role) for emergency access during an incident rather than having engineers punch ad hoc holes in production policies under pressure.
Kubernetes admission webhook outage: A v: Immediate restore: if the webhook is non-critical, patch its `failurePolicy` to `Ignore` or delete the ValidatingWebhookConfiguration to unblock the API server, since a blocking (`Fail`) policy on a broken webhook takes down all matching operations cluster-wide. Root-cause the actual timeout (webhook Pod crashed/unavailable, a certificate expired causing TLS handshake failure, or the webhook's own downstream dependency being slow) using the webhook's own logs and `kubectl describe` on its Deployment. Redesign for resilience: run the webhook with multiple replicas behind a Service (never a single replica for something this critical), set a reasonable `timeoutSeconds` so a slow webhook fails fast rather than hanging requests, monitor certificate expiry proactively, and maintain a documented break-glass procedure (temporarily setting `failurePolicy: Ignore`) for future incidents so this exact failure mode has a known, fast recovery path.
Kubernetes RBAC privilege escalation: Ho: Detect by auditing RBAC bindings for indirect escalation paths, not just direct high-privilege grants - the ability to create Pods with an arbitrary service account effectively grants that service account's permissions; `bind`/`escalate` verbs on roles let a user grant themselves broader roles; `impersonate` lets a user act as a more privileged identity; read access to Secrets in kube-system or other sensitive namespaces can expose credentials granting broader access. Tools like `kubectl-who-can` and RBAC audit tooling (e.g. rbac-lookup, or Kubernetes' own `auth can-i --list`) help enumerate these indirect paths systematically rather than manually reading role definitions. Prevent by following least-privilege rigorously (avoid wildcard verbs/resources), restricting `bind`/`escalate`/`impersonate` verbs to a very small trusted set of admin roles, and treating webhook-modification permissions as equivalent to cluster-admin, since a malicious webhook can intercept and alter any admission decision cluster-wide.
Kubernetes service account token securit: Move off the legacy auto-mounted long-lived Secret-based service account tokens (deprecated by default in modern Kubernetes) to projected, time-bound, audience-scoped tokens (`serviceAccountToken` volume projection) that Kubernetes automatically rotates and that are only valid for a specific audience (e.g. only accepted by a specific external API, not reusable elsewhere if leaked). For workloads needing to authenticate to external cloud APIs, use the cloud provider's workload identity federation (GKE Workload Identity, EKS IAM Roles for Service Accounts) so the Kubernetes service account token is exchanged for short-lived cloud credentials rather than a static key ever being stored at all. Disable automounting (`automountServiceAccountToken: false`) on Pods that don't actually need API server access, since an unused mounted token is pure unnecessary attack surface.
Kubernetes StatefulSet recovery: A zonal: The core constraint is that most cloud persistent disks are zonal - a Pod's PVC bound to a disk in the failed zone genuinely cannot be reattached elsewhere until that zone recovers, which is why StatefulSet DR design must plan for this upfront (via regional persistent disks, cross-zone replication at the application layer like a database's own replica set, or accepting a documented RPO for restore-from-backup). If quorum is lost with no surviving majority, the safe recovery path is restoring from the most recent backup/snapshot into new PVCs in a healthy zone, accepting data loss back to that backup point (the actual RPO), rather than attempting to force a quorum reformation with stale/inconsistent data, which risks silent data corruption. Recovery order matters: restore the StatefulSet's ordinal identity and storage first (in order, 0 before 1 before 2, respecting the application's own quorum-formation expectations) before scaling application-level traffic back onto it.
Kubernetes CSI failure: PVC provisioning: Check `kubectl describe pvc` and `describe pod` for the specific event chain first - it usually distinguishes provisioning failure (CSI controller plugin issue, StorageClass misconfiguration, or a cloud-side quota limit hit) from attachment failure (CSI node plugin issue, or a topology mismatch where the PV is in a different zone than the node the Pod is scheduled to). Check the CSI controller and node plugin Pods' own logs directly for the underlying cloud API error (often a quota exceeded, an IAM permission issue, or a transient cloud API error), and check for stuck finalizers on PVs/PVCs (a common cause of PVCs appearing to hang in Terminating indefinitely, requiring careful manual finalizer removal only once you've confirmed the underlying disk is actually safely detached).
Kubernetes CRD evolution: You own an ope: Introduce the new schema as a new API version (e.g. v1beta2 alongside existing v1beta1) rather than mutating the existing version in place, and implement a conversion webhook that translates between versions so clients using either version see consistent data. Set the storage version deliberately (only one version is ever the actual storage version at a time) and migrate stored objects to the new storage version via a controlled, monitored migration process (Kubernetes provides tooling to re-write all objects to trigger conversion and update the stored version) rather than a big-bang cutover. Keep the old version served (even if deprecated) for a transition period so existing clients/manifests don't break immediately, and always test the conversion webhook thoroughly against real stored object variations before rolling out broadly, since a conversion bug can corrupt or lose data across every object of that CRD type.
Kubernetes operator reconciliation: How: Design reconcile() to always compute the full desired state and diff against observed state on every run (never assume incremental/delta processing), so running it any number of times converges to the same correct result - true idempotency. Use finalizers to ensure cleanup logic runs before an object is actually deleted (removing the finalizer only after external resources are confirmed cleaned up), and status conditions to communicate reconciliation progress/health in a machine-readable, standard way other tooling can consume. Use leader election so only one controller replica actively reconciles at a time (avoiding duplicate/conflicting actions from multiple replicas racing), implement exponential backoff on requeue for failed reconciliations, and guard against hot loops (an object whose reconciliation itself triggers another immediate reconciliation, e.g. by updating its own status in a way that re-triggers the watch) by ensuring status updates don't spuriously re-trigger the same logic unnecessarily.
Kubernetes GitOps disaster recovery: Git: Order matters critically: provision the cluster infrastructure itself first (via Terraform, not GitOps, since GitOps needs a cluster to run on), then bootstrap the GitOps controller (ArgoCD/Flux) itself, then let it apply in dependency order - CRDs and their operators first (workloads referencing a CRD will fail if the CRD/operator isn't installed yet), then core platform services (ingress controller, cert-manager), then secrets (restored from your secrets backend/External Secrets Operator, since Git never held the actual secret values), and finally application workloads. Prove recovery objectives (RTO/RPO) by actually timing a full rebuild in a drill/game-day exercise rather than assuming it works from an architecture diagram - GitOps disaster recovery plans that have never been tested end-to-end reliably fail on exactly this kind of ordering dependency that isn't obvious until you actually try it.
Kubernetes multi-cluster failover: Desig: Active-active requires the application/data layer to genuinely support multi-region writes (a globally consistent database like Spanner, or an eventually-consistent design that tolerates conflicts) - without that, active-passive (one cluster serving traffic, the other on standby with replicated data) is the honest, simpler design most teams should default to. Traffic steering uses a global load balancer with health-check-based failover (DNS-based or an anycast/global LB); session state should be externalized (a shared cache/database, not in-memory per-instance) so failover doesn't drop user sessions; configuration drift between clusters is prevented by both clusters being managed from the same GitOps source rather than independently maintained. Failback (returning to the primary after it recovers) needs the same rigor as failover itself - reconciling any data written to the secondary during the outage before flipping traffic back, which is often the most overlooked and highest-risk part of the whole design.
Kubernetes noisy neighbor: One tenant ca: Apply ResourceQuotas per namespace (caps total resource consumption per tenant) and LimitRanges (enforces sane default/max requests-limits per Pod so one workload can't request unbounded resources), combined with a lower PriorityClass for less-critical tenant workloads so they're evicted first under node pressure. For genuinely noisy tenants, node-level isolation (a dedicated, tainted node pool for that tenant) removes shared-node contention entirely rather than relying on quotas alone to contain it. API Priority and Fairness protects the control plane specifically from one tenant's excessive API traffic starving others. Chargeback (cost/usage reporting per tenant based on actual consumption) creates an incentive structure that surfaces noisy-neighbor behavior to the responsible team directly, often resolving the behavioral root cause faster than purely technical controls alone.
Kubernetes forensic debugging: A contain: Establish these capture mechanisms proactively, before the next incident: centralized log shipping with retention (so a Pod's logs survive its deletion, since `kubectl logs` on a gone Pod returns nothing), Kubernetes audit logs capturing every API action with enough detail to reconstruct what happened and who/what triggered it, and event retention beyond Kubernetes' short default TTL (ship events to the same centralized logging system). For runtime-level forensics, configure core dump collection on crash (via a DaemonSet or node-level configuration) and consider a runtime security tool (Falco) that captures syscall-level activity in real time rather than only after the fact. Ephemeral containers (`kubectl debug`) let you attach a debug container to a still-running Pod's namespace for live investigation - but for a Pod that's already gone, none of this helps retroactively, which is exactly why all of this must be running continuously, not activated reactively after an incident already happened.
Jenkins shared library structure: How wo: `vars/` holds simple, directly-callable pipeline steps - each Groovy file (e.g. `vars/buildAndPush.groovy`) defines a `call()` method that becomes usable as a step name directly in any Jenkinsfile (`buildAndPush(image: 'myapp')`), ideal for straightforward reusable actions. `src/` holds structured Groovy classes (following standard Java/Groovy package conventions) for more complex logic - shared utility classes, data models, or logic too complex/reusable to cram into a single `vars/` script - which `vars/` scripts or Jenkinsfiles can then import and use, keeping complex logic testable and organized rather than all flattened into `vars/`.
Jenkins shared library versioning: How w: Tag releases in the shared library's Git repo (semantic versioning) and have consuming Jenkinsfiles pin to a specific tag (`@Library('common-pipeline@v2.3.0')`) rather than a floating branch like `@latest` or `@main` - this is the core safety mechanism, since it means a breaking change published to the library doesn't affect any pipeline until that pipeline's Jenkinsfile is explicitly updated to reference the new version. Roll out a breaking change by publishing it as a new major version tag, updating one or two low-risk consuming pipelines first to validate it works, then migrating other teams' Jenkinsfiles on their own schedule - never force-migrating everyone simultaneously by changing what a shared tag/branch points to.
Jenkins shared library testing: How woul: Use the Jenkins Pipeline Unit testing framework (a JUnit-based library specifically for testing Jenkins pipeline/shared-library Groovy code), which lets you mock Jenkins pipeline steps and DSL calls and assert on the logic's behavior without needing an actual running Jenkins instance - run these tests in a CI pipeline triggered on changes to the shared library repo itself, so a broken library change is caught before it's tagged/released, not discovered when it breaks a consuming team's production pipeline.
Jenkins shared library secrets: A shared: The shared library step should accept a Jenkins credentials ID as a parameter (not the secret value itself) and use `withCredentials`/`credentials()` binding inside the step to retrieve the actual secret at runtime from whichever Jenkins instance/Credentials store is executing the pipeline - this way the library code itself never contains or even sees a real secret value, and each consuming team/environment supplies their own credential ID pointing at their own stored credential, keeping the library fully reusable across different environments/teams without any shared secret coupling.
Global vs @Library shared library: What: A globally configured trusted shared library (configured by a Jenkins admin) is automatically available to every pipeline without any `@Library` annotation needed, and runs with full trust (no sandbox restrictions) - convenient, but any change affects every pipeline in the instance immediately with no per-team opt-in. A library explicitly loaded via `@Library('name@version')` in a specific Jenkinsfile is only available to that pipeline, at the exact version pinned, giving per-pipeline control over exactly which library version is used and when to adopt updates - the explicit approach is generally preferred in multi-team environments precisely because it avoids the 'everyone gets it whether ready or not' risk of global libraries.
Jenkins shared library parameters: How w: Design the step's `call()` method to accept a Map (named parameters) rather than positional arguments, with sensible defaults for anything most teams won't need to override: `def call(Map config) { def image = config.image; def namespace = config.namespace ?: 'default'; ... }`, invoked as `deployToKubernetes(image: 'myapp:v1', namespace: 'team-a')`. This lets each team's Jenkinsfile pass only the parameters relevant to them while sharing the exact same underlying deployment logic, and adding a new optional parameter later doesn't break any existing caller that doesn't pass it, since named parameters with defaults are inherently backward-compatible in a way positional arguments are not.
